newsitem.title: USA: Market says CFTC review speed-up not fast enough.
newsitem.headline: Market says CFTC review speed-up not fast enough.

text.p: A proposal by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to streamline its process for approving new futures contracts does not go far enough, futures exchanges and a leading legislator said.

"While the agency has taken a step in the right direction, the agency has still fallen short of providing the full regulatory relief needed," Patrick Arbor, chairman of the Chicago Board of Trade, said in a statement.
Sen. Richard Lugar, chairman of the Senate Agriculture Committee, said the CFTC proposal was "a good first step" but did not go as far as legislation he will offer next year.

Currently, it takes the CFTC about 90 days to approve new contracts for trading on U.S. futures exchanges. The exchanges argue that is too long, impeding their ability to compete with over-the-counter derivatives dealers and exchanges in other countries.
On Tuesday, the CFTC proposed creating a two-track approval process.

Under a so-called fast-track process, for contracts or amendments "which do not raise novel or complex issues," approval could be automatic after a brief review period, as few as 10 days, the CFTC said.
The Senators introduced a bill in the last Congress that would have allowed an exchange to begin trading any new contract after 10 days unless the CFTC stated it wanted to review the contract.
An exchange could begin trading after another 15 days unless the CFTC began proceedings to deny approval. The proceedings would have to be completed within 120 days.
"It is encouraging that the commission is moving in the direction of our legislation," Lugar said. "Although it doesn't go as far as our legislation, their proposal is a good first step."
Contracts raising more complicated issues could receive expedited reviews in 45 days, CFTC said. Review periods could be extended by 30 days.
Applications that appear to be at odds with the Commodity Exchange Act or commission rules could be amended or subject to a formal proceeding, at the exchange's option, the CFTC said.
Bipartisan legislation expected to be reintroduced early next year by Sen Lugar, the Indiania Republican, and Sen Patrick Leahy, Democrat from Vermont, would speed up the process even more.
Lugar said the bill would be a top priority of the Agriculture Committee next year.
Jack Sandner, chairman of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, said the exchange preferred the legislative solution.

"The CME and other U.S. futures exchanges need to innovate to stay alive," Sandner said in a statement. "The contract approval process spelled out in pending legislation will give us the flexibility we need to remain competitive."
CFTC officials have in the past said they had concerns about the Lugar-Leahy proposal to speed up contract approvals.
Brooksley Born, chairwoman of the commission, told Reuters in September that the approval proposal "seems quite cumbersome and perhaps unworkable."
